facts.claim: You do not need to be a New Zealand citizen; visitors to New Zealand can marry in New Zealand.
Before getting married you must apply for a marriage licence, which confirms it is legal for you to marry; a fee applies.
You need to arrange the licence at least 3 working days before you marry, and it expires after 3 months.
Anyone can apply for a marriage licence online, whether in New Zealand or not; a paper form is also available.
Only one of the couple needs to complete the application, but it needs information about both people.

Couples outside New Zealand use the notice of intended marriage form for parties ordinarily resident outside New Zealand (BDM 58): fill it in except the statutory declaration, sign the declaration in front of an authorised person listed on the form, and send the fee to Births, Deaths and Marriages.
When couples from outside New Zealand arrive in New Zealand, they need to visit a registry office to sign a declaration before the ceremony; addresses are on the application form.
Signing the declaration is not the wedding ceremony; you declare you are legally allowed to marry and have been truthful on the form.
You cannot legally marry if already married or in a civil union (unless changing the relationship with the same person), if closely related by birth, marriage or adoption, or if under 16.
For a personalised ceremony the couple is sent the licence and 2 copies of the Copy of Particulars of Marriage, and gives all 3 documents to the celebrant before the wedding.
You can only have the ceremony in the places you put on the licence application, so include a back-up venue.
Celebrants set their own fees on top of the licence fee.
In a personalised ceremony you choose the location and can marry on any day of the week, including weekends and public holidays, at any time.
You need to know your venue when you apply for the marriage licence.
A marriage cannot happen virtually: the couple, celebrant and witnesses must be physically present in the same place.
You need 2 witnesses who understand what is happening, can clearly identify both of you and are satisfied you both consent; they need not have known you for any length of time.
If the witnesses speak a different language, an interpreter is needed who signs a declaration before the ceremony.
The celebrant gives the couple a copy of particulars of marriage, which is not the same as a marriage certificate, and uses another copy to register the marriage with the New Zealand government.
Couples can write their own vows as long as each says words to the effect of 'I [name] take you [name] to be my legal wife/husband/partner'.
After the ceremony the couple and witnesses sign the 2 copies of the Copy of Particulars, the couple keeps one, and the celebrant sends the other to Births, Deaths and Marriages within 10 days.
If the place changes due to unforeseen circumstances, the new location must still be within New Zealand.
Australia is listed as an Apostille country for New Zealand documents.
Apostilles are done by the Department of Internal Affairs Authentication Unit; a paper apostille or an electronic e-apostille can be requested, so ask the Australian organisation which it wants.
The Authentication Unit processes apostille applications within 15 working days, with an urgent service within 5 working days for an extra fee; a fee applies.
Check whether the Authentication Unit needs an original or a notarised copy, and whether the organisation receiving it has its own requirements, such as recently issued documents.
